label: generalised2
title: Definition
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
An algebra $\langle A,\wedge,\vee,\rightarrow,0,1 \rangle$ of type $(2,2,2,0,0)$ is said to be a \textit{bounded distributive
hemi-implicative lattice} (h-lattice for short) if the algebra $(A,\wedge,\vee,\rightarrow,0,1)$ is a bounded distributive
lattice and the following two conditions are satisfied for every $a,b \in A$:
\begin{enumerate}[\normalfont 1)]
\item $a\rightarrow a = 1$,
\item $a\wedge (a\rightarrow b)\leq b$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

label: r1
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{r1}
Let $A\in \mathsf{hIL}$ and $a,b \in A$. Then the following conditions are satisfied:
\begin{enumerate}[\normalfont 1)]
\item If $a\rightarrow b = 1$, then $a\leq b$,
\item $a\rightarrow b = 1$ and $b\rightarrow a = 1$ if and only if $a = b$,
\item $a\wedge (a\leftrightarrow b) = b \wedge (a\leftrightarrow b)$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: It follows from a straightforward computation.

title: Example

title: Definition
head: environment

label: Kalman
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{Kalman}
If $A\in \mathsf{hIL}$ then $\mathrm{K}(A)\in \mathsf{KhIL}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $A\in \mathsf{hIL}$. We will show that $\mathrm{K}(A)$ satisfies the conditions of Definition
\ref{generalised2}. In order to prove it, let $x=(a,b)$, $y = (c,d)$ and $z = (e,f)$ be elements of $\mathrm{K}(A)$.

It is immediate that $x\rightarrow x = (1,0)$, so (hN1) 
is satisfied.

In order to show (hN2),  
note that
\[
x\wedge (x\rightarrow y) = (a\wedge (a\rightarrow c), b \vee (a\wedge d)),
\]
\[
x\wedge (\sim x \vee y) = (a\wedge (b\vee c), b\vee (a\wedge d)).
\]
Since $a\wedge (a\rightarrow c) \leq a\wedge c \leq a\wedge (b\vee c)$ then
\[
x\wedge (x\rightarrow y)\leq x\wedge (\sim x\vee y),
\]
so (hN2) is satisfied.

A direct computation shows that
\[
\sim(x\rightarrow y)\rightarrow (x\wedge \sim y) = (1,a\wedge d \wedge (b\vee c)).
\]
But 
\[
a\wedge d \wedge (b\vee c) = (a\wedge d \wedge b) \vee (a\wedge d \wedge c) = 0,
\]
so 
\[
\sim(x\rightarrow y)\rightarrow (x\wedge \sim y) = (1,0),
\]
which is (hN3).
            

Condition (hN4)
           
follows from the equality
\[
(x\wedge \sim y)\rightarrow \sim(x\rightarrow y) = (1, a\wedge d\wedge (a\rightarrow c))
\]
and the fact that $a\wedge d\wedge (a\rightarrow c) \leq c\wedge d = 0$, i.e.,
$a\wedge d\wedge (a\rightarrow c) = 0$.

Now we will show (hN5) and (hN6).
                          
Straightforward computations
show that
\begin{equation} \label{a1}
x\wedge y\wedge (x\rightarrow y) = (a\wedge c\wedge (a\rightarrow c),b\vee d),
\end{equation}
\begin{equation} \label{a2}
x\wedge (x\rightarrow y) = (a\wedge (a\rightarrow c), b\vee (a\wedge d)).
\end{equation}
Besides, 
$a\wedge (a\rightarrow c)\leq a\wedge c\wedge (a\rightarrow c)$, so
\begin{equation} \label{a3}
a\wedge c\wedge (a\rightarrow c) = a\wedge (a\rightarrow c).
\end{equation} 
Moreover, taking into account the distributivity of the underlying 
lattice of $A$ and the facts that $a\wedge b = c\wedge d = 0$ and $a\wedge (a\rightarrow c)\leq c$, 
we get
\begin{equation} \label{a4}
(a\wedge c\wedge (a\rightarrow c))\wedge (b\vee (a\wedge d)) = 0,
\end{equation}
\begin{equation} \label{a5}
(a\wedge (a\rightarrow c))\wedge (b\vee d) = 0.
\end{equation}
Thus, a direct computation based on equations (\ref{a1}),\dots,(\ref{a5}) shows that conditions
(hN5) and (hN6)
                         
are satisfied.

Suppose that $x\rightarrow y = 1$, $y\rightarrow x = 1$, $y\rightarrow z = 1$ and $z\rightarrow y = 1$, so
$a\rightarrow c = 1$, $a\wedge d = 0$, $c\rightarrow a = 1$, $c\wedge b = 0$, $c\rightarrow e = 1$,
$c\wedge f = 0$, $e\rightarrow c = 1$ and $e\wedge d = 0$. In particular, it follows
from Lemma \ref{r1} that $a = c = e$, so
\[
x \rightarrow z = (1,a\wedge f).
\]
However, $a\wedge f =  e\wedge f = 0$.
Hence, $x\rightarrow z = (1,0)$. Analogously, we have that $z\rightarrow x = (1,0)$.
Thus, (hN7) 
              
is satisfied.

Finally, we will show (hN8) and (hN9).
                                  
Suppose that $x\rightarrow y = 1$ and $y\rightarrow x = 1$,
so $a = c$, $a\wedge d = 0$ and $c\wedge b = 0$. Besides,
\[
x\wedge z = (a\wedge e,b\vee f),
\]
\[
y\wedge z = (c\wedge e,d\vee f) = (a\wedge e,d\vee f),
\]
which implies that
\[
(x\wedge z) \rightarrow (y\wedge z) = (1,a\wedge e\wedge (d\vee f)).
\]
Since $a\wedge e\wedge (d\vee f) = (a\wedge e\wedge d) \vee (a\wedge e \wedge f)$ and $a = c$ then
$a\wedge e\wedge (d\vee f) = 0$, so
\[
(x\wedge z) \rightarrow (y\wedge z) = (1,0),
\]
which is (hN8).
                
In order to see (hN9),
                 
note that
\[
x\vee z = (a\vee e,b\wedge f),
\]
\[
(c\vee e,d\wedge f) = (a\vee e,d\wedge f),
\]
so 
\[
(x\vee z) \rightarrow (y\vee z) = (1,(a\vee e)\wedge d\wedge f).
\]
Taking into account that $(a\vee e)\wedge d\wedge f = (a \wedge d \wedge f) \vee (e\wedge d\wedge f)$,
$a = c$, $a\wedge c = 0$ and $e\wedge f = 0$ we get 
\[
(a\vee e)\wedge d\wedge f = 0. 
\]
Therefore,
\[
(x\vee z) \rightarrow (y\vee z) = (1,0),
\]
which was our aim.
head: environment

label: pvi
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{pvi}
Let $T\in \mathsf{KhIL}$.
The following conditions are satisfied for every $x,y\in T$:
\begin{enumerate}[\normalfont 1)]
\item $1\rightarrow x\leq x$,
\item if $x\rightarrow y = 1$ then $x = x\wedge (\sim x \vee y)$,
\item if $x\rightarrow y = 1$ and $\sim y\rightarrow \sim x = 1$ then $x\leq y$. 
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
First we will show that condition 1) is satisfied. By (hN2), 
                                           
\[
(1\rightarrow x)=1\wedge (1\rightarrow x)\leq 1\wedge(\sim 1 \vee x)=x, i.e.,
\]
$1\rightarrow x \leq x$.

Now we will show that 2) is verified. Suppose that $x\rightarrow y = 1$, so by (hN2)
                                          
we get $x\leq (\sim x\vee y)$, i.e., 
\[
x = x\wedge (\sim x \vee y). 
\]

Finally we will see 3) is satisfied. Assume that $x\rightarrow y = 1$ and $\sim y\rightarrow \sim x = 1$.
It follows from 2. of this proposition that
\[
x = x\wedge (\sim x \vee y) = (x\wedge \sim x) \vee (x\wedge y),
\]
\[
\sim y = \sim y \wedge (y \vee \sim x) =(\sim y\wedge y)\vee (\sim y \wedge \sim x),
\]
so
\[
y = (y\vee \sim y) \wedge (x\vee y).
\]
In particular,
\[
x =(x\wedge \sim x)\vee (x\wedge y) \leq (y\vee \sim y) \vee (x\wedge y) = y\vee \sim y,
\]
so
\[
x = x\wedge (x\vee y) \leq (y\vee \sim y) \wedge (x\vee y) = y.
\]
Therefore, $x\leq y$.

label: example2
title: Example
head: environment

label: l1
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{l1}
Let $T\in \mathsf{KhIL}$. Then $\theta$ is an equivalence relation compatible with $\wedge$, $\vee$ and $\rightarrow$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The reflexivity and symmetry of $\theta$ are immediate. The transitivity of the relation
follows from (hN7).
                                              
Thus, $\theta$ is an equivalence relation.
The facts that $\theta$ is compatible with $\wedge$, $\vee$ and $\rightarrow$ follow from (hN8), (hN9) and (hN10).
head: environment

title: Proposition
body_md: If $T\in \mathsf{KhIL}$ then $T/\theta \in \mathsf{hIL}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $T\in \mathsf{KhIL}$ and $x,y\in T$. It follows from (hN1)                                           
that 
\[
x/\theta \rightarrow x/\theta = 1/\theta. 
\]
The inequality 
\[
x/\theta \wedge (x/\theta \rightarrow y/\theta) \preceq y/\theta
\] 
follows from (hN5) and (hN6).
                                                         
Therefore, $T/\theta \in \mathsf{hIL}$.
head: environment

label: rept
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{rept}
Let $T\in \mathsf{KhIL}$. Then the map $\rho_T:T\rightarrow \mathrm{K}(T/\theta)$ given by $\rho_{T}(x) = (x/\theta,\sim x/\theta)$ is a monomorphism.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We write $\rho$ instead of $\rho_T$.
First we will show that $\rho$ is a well defined map. Let $x\in T$.
Note that $x/\theta \wedge \sim x/\theta = 0/\theta$ if and only if $(x\wedge \sim x) \rightarrow 0 = 1$
and $0\rightarrow (x\wedge \sim x) = 1$. First note that it follows from (hN1) and (hN4)
                                                         
that
\[
(x\wedge \sim x) \rightarrow 0 = (x\wedge \sim x) \rightarrow \sim (x\rightarrow x) = 1.
\]
Besides, it follows from (hN1) and (hN3)
                                                         
that
\[
0\rightarrow (x\wedge \sim x) = \sim (x\rightarrow x) \rightarrow (x\wedge \sim x) = 1.
\]
Thus, $\rho$ is a well defined map.

Straightforward computations show that $\rho$ preserves $\wedge$, $\vee$, $\sim$, $0$ and $1$.
The fact that $\rho$ preserves $\rightarrow$ follows from (hN3) and (hN4).
                                                         
Hence, $\rho$ is a homomorphism. 
Finally, in order to show that $\rho$ is an injective map let $x,y \in T$ such
that $\rho(x) = \rho(y)$, i.e., $x\rightarrow y= 1$, $y\rightarrow x = 1$, $\sim x \rightarrow \sim y = 1$ and $\sim y \rightarrow \sim x = 1$.
Thus, it follows from Lemma \ref{pvi} that $x = y$. Hence, $\rho$ is an injective map.
Therefore, $\rho$ is a monomorphism.
head: environment

label: eq neg
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $A\in \mathsf{hIL}$. We show that equation~\eqref{eq n} holds in $\mathrm{K}(A)$. 
Take $x=(a,b)$, $y=(c,d)$ and $z=(e,f)$ in $\mathrm{K}(A)$. Then
\[
(x\rightarrow y)\vee (z\wedge \sim z)
  = (a\rightarrow c,\,(a\wedge d)\wedge (e\vee f)),
\]
and
\[
(x\vee (z\wedge \sim z))\rightarrow (y\vee (z\wedge \sim z))
  = (a,\, b\wedge (e\vee f))\rightarrow (c,\, d\wedge (e\vee f)).
\]
It is straightforward to verify that
\[
(a,\, b\wedge (e\vee f))\rightarrow (c,\, d\wedge (e\vee f))
   = (a\rightarrow c,\,(a\wedge d)\wedge (e\vee f)).
\]
Thus equation~\eqref{eq n} holds in $\mathrm{K}(A)$.

Finally, by Theorem~\ref{rept}, every $T\in \mathsf{KhIL}$ is isomorphic to a subalgebra of 
$\mathrm{K}(A)$ for some $A\in \mathsf{hIL}$, and hence equation~\eqref{eq n} holds in $T$ as well.
head: environment

label: kleene cond
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose that $1 = x \vee (z \wedge \sim z)$. It follows that $1\leq x \vee \sim z$, and by De Morgan’s laws we obtain
    $\sim x \wedge z = 0$.  
    Since $z \wedge \sim z \leq x \vee \sim x$, we have $x \vee (z \wedge \sim z) \leq x \vee \sim x$, which implies $x \vee \sim x = 1$.  
    Therefore,
    \[
    z = z \wedge (x \vee \sim x)
      = (z \wedge x) \vee (z \wedge \sim x)
      = (z \wedge x) \vee 0
      = z \wedge x.
    \]
    Hence $z \leq x$, and consequently $1 = x \vee z = x$. 
    The converse implication is immediate and the result follows.
head: environment

label: equivalence eq
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose that $x \rightarrow y = 1$ and $y \rightarrow x = 1$.  
From Proposition~\ref{pvi} we obtain $x = x \wedge (\sim x \vee y)$ and
$y = y \wedge (\sim y \vee x)$.
Let $z = (x \wedge \sim x) \vee (y \wedge \sim y)$.  
Then $z \leq \sim z$ and $z \wedge \sim z = z$.  
Hence,
\[ x \vee z
   = x \vee (x \wedge \sim x) \vee (y \wedge \sim y)
   = x \vee (y \wedge \sim y)
   = (x \vee y) \wedge (x \vee \sim y).
\]
Since $y \leq \sim y \vee x$, we have
$x \vee y \leq \sim y \vee x$,
and therefore $x \vee (z \wedge \sim z) = x \vee y$.
By the same reasoning, $y \vee (z \wedge \sim z) = x \vee y$,
and thus, $y \vee (z \wedge \sim z) = x \vee (z \wedge \sim z)$.

Now, suppose that there exists $z\in T$ such that $x\vee (z\wedge\sim z)=y\vee (z\wedge\sim z)$. By (hN1) and (\ref{eq n}), $1=x\vee (z\wedge\sim z)\rightarrow y\vee (z\wedge\sim z)=(x\rightarrow y)\vee (z\wedge\sim z)$. By Lemma \ref{kleene cond}, $x\rightarrow y=1$. By the same reasoning we obtain $y\rightarrow x=1$.
head: environment

title: Theorem
body_md: The class $\mathsf{KhIL}$ is a variety.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We will prove that $\mathsf{KhIL}$ is precisely the class of algebras defined by the equations of Kleene algebras together with conditions (hN1)–(hN6) and equation (\ref{eq n}). 

On the one hand, from Proposition~\ref{eq neg} it follows that every algebra in 
$\mathsf{KhIL}$ satisfies equation (\ref{eq n}).

On the other hand, assume that $T$ satisfies conditions~(hN1)--(hN6) and equation (\ref{eq n}). From Proposition \ref{equivalence eq} it follows immediately that $T$ satisfies conditions (hN8), (hN9) and (hN7), since $\theta_{T^-}$ is a lattice congruence of $T$.

To prove condition (hN10), suppose that $x\rightarrow y=y\rightarrow x=1$. By Proposition \ref{equivalence eq}, there exists $w\in T$ such that $x\vee (w\wedge\sim w)=y\vee (w\wedge\sim w)$. Then, 
\[z\vee (w\wedge\sim w)\rightarrow x\vee (w\wedge\sim w)=z\vee (w\wedge\sim w)\rightarrow y\vee (w\wedge\sim w)\]
and by equation (\ref{eq n}), it follows that
\[(z\rightarrow x)\vee (w\wedge\sim w)=(z\rightarrow y)\vee (w\wedge\sim w).\]
Again, by Proposition \ref{equivalence eq}, $(z\rightarrow x)\rightarrow (z\rightarrow y)=1$ and $(z\rightarrow y)\rightarrow (z\rightarrow x)=1$. Analogously, it is proved that $(y\rightarrow z)\rightarrow (x\rightarrow z)=1$ and $(x\rightarrow z)\rightarrow (y\rightarrow z)=1$. Therefore, $T\in \mathsf{KhIL}$ and the result follows.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
Equation (\ref{eq n}) is independent from Conditions (hN1)-(hN6). To see this, let us consider the chain $T=\{0,a,1\}$ where $0<a<1$ and the operation $\rightarrow$ is defined by
	\begin{center}
	\begin{tabular}{|c|c|c|c|}
		\hline
		$\rightarrow$& $0$ & $a$ & $1$ \\
		\hline
		$0$ & $1$ & $1$ & $1$ \\
		\hline
		$a$ & $1$ & $1$ & $a$ \\
		\hline
		$1$ & $0$ & $a$ & $1$ \\
		\hline
	\end{tabular}
	\end{center}
    and $\sim 0=1$, $\sim 1=0$ and $\sim a=a$. $T$ is a Kleene algebra that satisfies Conditions (hN1)-(hN6) but
    \[(0\rightarrow 1)\vee a=1\vee a=1\neq (0\vee a\rightarrow 1\vee a)=(a\rightarrow 1)=a.\]
head: environment

label: gf
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{gf}
Let $T\in \mathsf{KhIL}$ and $F\subseteq T$. 
We say that $F$ is an \textit{h-implicative filter} of $T$ if it is an implicative filter of $T$ which
satisfies the following additional conditions for every $x,y\in T$ and $f\in F$:
\begin{enumerate}[\normalfont F1)]
\item $(x\rightarrow y)\rightarrow ((x\wedge f)\rightarrow (y\wedge f))\in F$,
\item $((x\wedge f)\rightarrow (y\wedge f)) \rightarrow (x\rightarrow y)\in F$,
\item $\sim (x\rightarrow y)\rightarrow \sim ((x\wedge f)\rightarrow (y\wedge f))\in F$,
\item $\sim ((x\wedge f)\rightarrow (y\wedge f)) \rightarrow \sim (x\rightarrow y)\in F$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

label: remark18
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{remark18}
Let $T\in \mathsf{KhIL}$ and $F\in \mathrm{hIF}(T)$. Then $F$ is an upset.
Indeed, let $x, y\in T$ such that $x\leq y$ and $x\in F$.
It follows from F2) that $((x\wedge x)\rightarrow (y\wedge x)) \rightarrow (x\rightarrow y)\in F$,
i.e., $1\rightarrow (x\rightarrow y) \in F$. Since $1\in F$ then $x\rightarrow y \in F$.
Taking into account that $x\in F$ we get $y\in F$. Therefore, $F$ is an upset.
head: environment

label: lc2
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lc2}
Let $T\in \mathsf{KhIL}$ and $\theta \in \mathrm{Con}(T)$. Then $1/\theta \in \mathrm{hIF}(T)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\theta \in \mathrm{Con}(T)$. Note that $1/\theta$ is an upset because
$\theta$ is in particular a lattice congruence. In order to show that $1/\theta$ is an implicative 
filter, let $x,y\in T$ such that $x, x\rightarrow y\in 1/\theta$. Then $x \wedge (x\rightarrow y)\in 1/\theta$.
Since $1/\theta$ is an upset then it follows from (hN2)
            
that $x \wedge (\sim x \vee y) \in 1/\theta$.
Moreover, since $x/\theta = 1/\theta$ then $\sim x/\theta = 0/\theta$, so $y/\theta = 1/\theta$, i.e.,
$y\in 1/\theta$. Hence, $1/\theta$ is an implicative filter. The fact that $1/\theta$ is an 
h-implicative filter follows from a direct computation.
head: environment

label: lc3
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\theta \in \mathrm{Con}(T)$ and $x,y \in T$. It is immediate that if $(x,y)\in \theta$ then
$x\rightarrow y$, $\sim y \rightarrow \sim x$, $y\rightarrow x$, $\sim x \rightarrow \sim y \in 1/\theta$.
Conversely, assume that $x\rightarrow y$, $\sim y \rightarrow \sim x$, $y\rightarrow x$, $\sim x \rightarrow \sim y \in 1/\theta$.
Since $T/\theta \in \mathsf{KhIL}$ then it follows from Proposition \ref{pvi} that
$x/\theta = y/\theta$, i.e., $(x,y)\in \theta$.
head: environment

label: lc4
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\theta,\psi \in \mathrm{Con}(T)$. It is immediate that if $\theta\subseteq \psi$ then
$1/\theta \subseteq 1/\psi$. The converse follows from a direct computation based in Lemma \ref{lc3}.
head: environment

label: lc5
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
It follows from the definition of implicative filter that $1\in F$. From F2), in Remark \ref{remark18}, it follows that $F$ is an upset.
Now, let $x\in T$. In order to show that $x\in F$ if and only if $1\rightarrow x\in F$,
suppose that $x\in F$. Then
\[
1\rightarrow (1\rightarrow x) = ((1\wedge x)\rightarrow (x\wedge x))\rightarrow (1\rightarrow x)\in F,
\]
so $1\rightarrow x\in F$. The converse follows from Proposition \ref{pvi}.

Finally, in order to show that $F$ is closed by $\wedge$, let
$x, y \in F$.
Then
$1\rightarrow y\in F$. Moreover,
\[
(1\rightarrow y) \rightarrow ((1\wedge x) \rightarrow (y\wedge x))\in F
\]
because $x\in F$, so since $1\rightarrow y \in F$
then $x\rightarrow (y\wedge x)\in F$. Thus, $y\wedge x\in F$.
Hence, $F$ is a filter.
head: environment

label: lc6
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lc6}
Let $T\in \mathsf{KhIL}$ and $x,y,z\in T$. Then the following conditions are satisfied:
\begin{enumerate}[\normalfont 1)]
\item $(x\wedge (x\leftrightarrow y)) \rightarrow (y\wedge (x\leftrightarrow y)) = 1$,
\item $(x\wedge s(x,y)) \rightarrow (y\wedge s(x,y)) = 1$,
\item $(x\wedge (x\leftrightarrow y)\wedge (y\leftrightarrow z)) \rightarrow (z\wedge (x\leftrightarrow y)\wedge (y\leftrightarrow z)) = 1$,
\item $(x\wedge s(x,y) \wedge s(y,z)) \rightarrow (z\wedge s(x,y)\wedge s(y,z)) = 1$,
\item $((x\vee z)\wedge (x\leftrightarrow y)) \rightarrow ((y\vee z) \wedge (x\leftrightarrow y)) = 1$,
\item $(x\wedge s(x,y))\rightarrow (z\wedge s(x,y)) = (y\wedge s(x,y))\rightarrow (z\wedge s(x,y))$,
\item $(z\wedge s(x,y)) \rightarrow (x\wedge s(x,y)) = (z\wedge s(x,y)) \rightarrow (y\wedge s(x,y))$,
\item $((z\wedge (x\leftrightarrow y)) \rightarrow (x\wedge (x\leftrightarrow y))) \rightarrow ((z\wedge (x\leftrightarrow y)) \rightarrow (y\wedge (x\leftrightarrow y))) = 1$,
\item $((x\wedge (x\leftrightarrow y)) \rightarrow (z\wedge (x\leftrightarrow y))) \rightarrow ((y\wedge (x\leftrightarrow y)) \rightarrow (z\wedge (x\leftrightarrow y))) = 1$,
\item $(x\wedge \sim x) \rightarrow 0 = 0 \rightarrow (x\wedge \sim x) = 1$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Theorem \ref{rept} without loss of generality we can assume that $T = \mathrm{K}(A)$ for
some $A\in \mathsf{hIL}$. Let $x = (a,b)$, $y = (c,d)$ and $z = (e,f)$ be elements of $\mathrm{K}(A)$. 
A direct computation shows that
\[
x\leftrightarrow y = (a\leftrightarrow c, (a\wedge d)\vee (c\wedge b)),
\]
\[
\sim x \leftrightarrow \sim y = (b\leftrightarrow d, (a\wedge d)\vee (c\wedge b)),
\]
\[
y\leftrightarrow z = (c\leftrightarrow e, (c\wedge f) \vee (e\wedge d)),
\]
\[
\sim y \leftrightarrow \sim z = (d\leftrightarrow f, (c\wedge f) \vee (e\wedge d)),
\]
so
\[
s(x,y) = ((a\leftrightarrow c) \wedge (b\leftrightarrow d), (a\wedge d)\vee (c\wedge b)).
\]
In order to show 1) note that
\[
x\wedge (x\leftrightarrow y) = (a \wedge (a\leftrightarrow c), b\vee (a\wedge d)),
\]
\[
y \wedge (x\leftrightarrow y) = (c\wedge (a\leftrightarrow c), d\vee (c\wedge b)).
\]
Since $a \wedge (a\leftrightarrow c) = c\wedge (a\leftrightarrow c)$,
a direct computation proves that
\[
(x\wedge (x\leftrightarrow y)) \rightarrow (y\wedge (x\leftrightarrow y)) = (1,0).
\]

The conditions 2) follows from 1) of this lemma and (hN8).
                                               

In order to show the condition 3), note that it follows from 1) of this lemma
and (hN8)
                                               
that
\[
(x\wedge (x\leftrightarrow y)\wedge (y\leftrightarrow z)) \rightarrow (y\wedge (x\leftrightarrow y)\wedge (y\leftrightarrow z) )= 1,
\]
\[
(y\wedge (x\leftrightarrow y)\wedge (y\leftrightarrow z)) \rightarrow (z\wedge (x\leftrightarrow y)\wedge (y\leftrightarrow z)) = 1.
\]
Hence, it follows from (hN7) 
              
that 
\[
(x\wedge (x\leftrightarrow y)\wedge (y\leftrightarrow z)) \rightarrow (z\wedge (x\leftrightarrow y)\wedge (y\leftrightarrow z)) = 1.
\]

The condition 4) follows from 3) of this lemma and (hN8).
                                               

The condition 5) follows from 1) of this lemma, the distributivity of the
underlying lattice of $T$ and (hN9).
                                                

In order to show 6), note that
\[
x\wedge s(x,y) = (a\wedge (a\leftrightarrow c) \wedge (b\leftrightarrow d),b \vee (a\wedge d)),
\]
\[
y\wedge s(x,y) = (c\wedge (a\leftrightarrow c)\wedge (b\leftrightarrow d), d\vee (c\wedge b)),
\]
\[
z\wedge s(x,y) = (e\wedge (a\leftrightarrow c)\wedge (b\leftrightarrow d), f \vee (a\wedge d)\vee (c\wedge b)).
\]
Given $(u,v) \in T$ we define $\pi_1(u,v) = u$ and $\pi_2(u,v) = v$.
It is immediate that $\pi_1(x\wedge s(x,y)) = \pi_1(y\wedge s(x,y))$,
so 
\[
\pi_1((x\wedge s(x,y)) \rightarrow (z\wedge s(x,y))) = \pi_1((y\wedge s(x,y)) \rightarrow (z\wedge s(x,y))).
\]
Besides, a direct computation shows that 
\[
\pi_2(x\wedge s(x,y)) \rightarrow (z\wedge s(x,y)) = f\wedge a\wedge (a\leftrightarrow c)\wedge (b\leftrightarrow d),
\] 
\[
\pi_2((y\wedge s(x,y)) \rightarrow (z\wedge s(x,y)) = f\wedge c\wedge (a\leftrightarrow c)\wedge (b\leftrightarrow d).
\]
Since $a\wedge (a\leftrightarrow c) = c\wedge (a\leftrightarrow c)$ then 
\[
f\wedge a\wedge (a\leftrightarrow c)\wedge (b\leftrightarrow d) = f\wedge c\wedge (a\leftrightarrow c)\wedge (b\leftrightarrow d).
\]
Thus, we have proved 6). A similar argument shows 7). 

The conditions 8) and 9) follow from 1) of this lemma and (hN10).
                                            

Condition 10) follows from a direct computation.
head: environment

label: lc7
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lc7}
Let $T\in \mathsf{KhIL}$ and $F\in \mathrm{hIF}(T)$. Then $\Theta(F)$ is an equivalence relation such that $1/\Theta(F) = F$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $F\in \mathrm{hIF}(T)$. First we will show that $\Theta(F)$ is an equivalence relation.
It is immediate that $\Theta(F)$ is a reflexive and symmetric relation. In order to show the
transitivity, let $x,y,z\in T$ such that $(x,y), (y,z) \in \Theta(F)$, i.e., $s(x,y), s(y,z) \in F$.
Let $f = s(x,y)\wedge s(y,z)$. It follows from Lemma \ref{lc5} that $F$ is a filter, so $f\in F$.
Besides it follows from Lemma \ref{lc6} that $(x\wedge f) \rightarrow (z\wedge f) = 1$.
But $((x\wedge f) \rightarrow (z\wedge f)) \rightarrow (x\rightarrow z)\in F$,  so $x\rightarrow z \in F$.
Similarly we have that $z\rightarrow x\in, \sim x \rightarrow \sim z, \sim z\rightarrow \sim x \in F$.
Thus, $s(x,z)\in F$, i.e., $(x,z)\in \Theta(F)$. Hence, $\Theta(F)$ is a transitive relation.
In consequence, $\Theta(F)$ is an equivalence relation.

Finally, let $x\in T$. Then $x\in 1/\Theta(F)$ if and only if $x\rightarrow 1, 1\rightarrow x, 0\rightarrow \sim x$ and $\sim x\rightarrow 0 \in F$.
Suppose that $x\rightarrow 1, 1\rightarrow x, 0\rightarrow \sim x$ and $\sim x\rightarrow 0 \in F$. Since $1\rightarrow x\in F$ then it follows from 
Lemma \ref{lc5} that $x\in F$. Conversely, assume that $x\in F$. It follows from Lemma \ref{lc5} that $1\rightarrow x\in F$.
Besides, $((x\wedge x)\rightarrow (1\wedge x))\rightarrow (x\rightarrow 1) \in F$, i.e., $1\rightarrow (x\rightarrow 1) \in F$, so $x\rightarrow 1 \in F$.
Moreover, it follows from Lemma \ref{lc6} that $0\rightarrow (\sim x \wedge x) = 1$.
Since $((0\wedge x) \rightarrow (\sim x \wedge x)) \rightarrow (0\rightarrow \sim x)\in F$ then $0\rightarrow \sim x \in F$.
Finally, since $(\sim x \wedge x) \rightarrow 0 = 1$ and $((\sim x \wedge x)\rightarrow (0\wedge x))\rightarrow (\sim x \rightarrow 0) \in F$ then
$\sim x \rightarrow 0 \in F$. Therefore, $1/\Theta(F) = F$.
head: environment

label: lc8
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lc8}
Let $T\in \mathsf{KhIL}$ and $F\in \mathrm{hIF}(T)$. Then $\Theta(F) \in \mathrm{Con}(T)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
First we will see that $\Theta(F)$ preserves $\wedge$. Let $x,y,z\in T$ such that $(x,y) \in \Theta(F)$, i.e., $s(x,y)\in F$.
It follows from Lemma \ref{lc6} that 
\[
(x\wedge s(x,y)) \rightarrow (y\wedge s(x,y)) = 1,
\]
\[
(y\wedge s(x,y)) \rightarrow (x\wedge s(x,y)) = 1. 
\]
Thus, it follows from (hN8)
                                               
that 
\[
(x\wedge z\wedge s(x,y)) \rightarrow (y\wedge z\wedge s(x,y)) = 1. 
\]
But 
\[
((x\wedge z\wedge s(x,y)) \rightarrow (y\wedge z\wedge s(x,y))) \rightarrow ((x\wedge z) \rightarrow (y\wedge z))\in F, 
\]
so $(x\wedge z) \rightarrow (y\wedge z) \in F$. Similarly, $(y\wedge z)\rightarrow (x\wedge z)\in F$.
In order to show that $\sim(x\wedge z) \rightarrow \sim(y\wedge z) \in F$, first 
note that 
\[
(\sim x\wedge s(x,y)) \rightarrow (\sim y\wedge s(x,y)) = 1,
\]
\[
(\sim y\wedge s(x,y)) \rightarrow (\sim x\wedge s(x,y)) = 1,
\]
so it follows from (hN9)
                                                 
that
\[
(((\sim x\wedge s(x,y)) \vee (\sim z \wedge s(x,y))) \rightarrow((\sim y\wedge s(x,y)) \vee (\sim z \wedge s(x,y))) = 1,
\]
i.e.,
\[
(\sim (x\wedge z) \wedge s(x,y)) \rightarrow (\sim (y\wedge z)\wedge s(x,y)) = 1.
\]
Hence, $\sim (x\wedge z) \rightarrow \sim(y\wedge z) \in F$. Analogously, we get 
$\sim (y\wedge z) \rightarrow \sim(x\wedge z) \in F$. Thus, $(x\wedge z,y\wedge z) \in \Theta(F)$.

It follows from that $s(x,y) = s(\sim x, \sim y)$ the fact that $\Theta(F)$ preserves $\sim$.
Since we have also proved that $\Theta(F)$ preserves $\wedge$ and in particular $T$ is a
Kleene algebra, then $\Theta(F)$ preserves $\vee$.

In what follows we will show that $\Theta(F)$ preserves the implication. Let $x,y,z\in T$
such that $(x,y)\in \Theta(F)$, i.e., $s(x,y) \in F$.
Then 
\[
(x\rightarrow z, ((x\wedge s(x,y))\rightarrow (z\wedge s(x,y))),
\]
\[
(y\rightarrow z, ((y\wedge s(x,y))\rightarrow (z\wedge s(x,y)))
\]
are elements of $\Theta(F)$. Since it follows from Lemma \ref{lc6}
that 
\[
(x\wedge s(x,y))\rightarrow (z\wedge s(x,y)) = (y\wedge s(x,y))\rightarrow (z\wedge s(x,y))
\]
then the transitivity of $\Theta(F)$ implies that $(x\rightarrow z,y\rightarrow z) \in \Theta(F)$.
A similar argument based on Lemma \ref{lc6} shows that $(z\rightarrow x,z\rightarrow y)\in \Theta(F)$.
Hence, $\Theta(F)$ preserves the implication.

Then, $T/\Theta(F) \in \mathsf{KhIL}$. Therefore, $\Theta(F) \in \mathrm{Con}(T)$.
head: environment

label: thm-con
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
An implicative filter $F$ of an h-Nelson algebra is said to be \textit{open} if $1\rightarrow x \in F$
whenever $x\in F$.
head: environment

label: open-if
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{open-if}
Let $T\in \mathsf{KhIL}$. Then every h-implicative filter of $T$ is an open implicative filter of $T$.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
Let $T\in \mathsf{KhIL}$ and $F\subseteq T$. We say that $F$ is an \textit{N-implicative filter}
if $1\in F$ and for every $x,y \in T$ it holds that if $x, x\rightarrow_N \in F$ then $y\in F$.
head: environment

label: rem-Nsd
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem-Nsd}
Let $T\in \mathsf{KhIL}$ and $F$ an $N$-implicative filter. Then $F$ is an upset.
Indeed, let $x\leq y$ and $x\in F$. Since $x\rightarrow_N y = 1\in F$ and $x\in F$ then $y\in F$.
Thus, $F$ is an upset.
head: environment

label: N-ds
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{N-ds}
Let $T\in \mathsf{KhIL}$. Then every h-implicative filter of $T$ is an N-implicative filter of $T$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $T\in \mathsf{KhIL}$. Let us take $F$ an h-implicative filter of $T$ and $x, x\rightarrow_N y \in F$.
In particular, $x\rightarrow (x\wedge y) \in F$. Then it follows from F2) that 
$((x\wedge x) \rightarrow (y\wedge x)) \rightarrow (x\rightarrow y)\in F$, i.e.,
$(x\rightarrow (x\wedge y)) \rightarrow (x\rightarrow y) \in F$. Thus, taking into account that $F$ is an implicative filter
and $x, x\rightarrow (x\wedge y) \in F$ we get $y\in F$. Therefore, $F$ is an 
N-implicative filter of $T$.
head: environment

label: rem-c
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem-c}
\
\begin{enumerate}[\normalfont 1)]
\item Note that if $T, U$ are Kleene algebras, $T$ has a center $\mathsf{c}_T$ and $f$ is a morphism in $\mathsf{KhIL}$ from $T$ to $U$, then 
$U$ has a center $\mathsf{c}_U$ and $f(\mathsf{c}_T) = \mathsf{c}_U$. Indeed, $f(\mathsf{c}_T) = f(\sim \mathsf{c}_T) = \sim f(\mathsf{c}_T)$.
\item If $T\in \mathsf{KhIL}^{c}$ then it follows from Theorem \ref{rept} and 1) that the map
$\rho_T:T\rightarrow \mathrm{K}(T/\theta)$ is a monomorphism in $\mathsf{KhIL}^{c}$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

label: ce1
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{ce1}
Let $T\in \mathsf{KhIL}^{c}$ and $x,y \in T$.
\begin{enumerate}[\normalfont 1)]
\item If $x\rightarrow y = 1$ then $x\vee \mathsf{c} \leq y\vee \mathsf{c}$.
\item If $x\vee \mathsf{c} = y\vee \mathsf{c}$ then $x\rightarrow y = 1$.
\item  $\mathsf{c} \rightarrow 0 = 1$. 
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
It follows from Remark \ref{rem-c} that without loss of generality we can assume that $T = \mathrm{K}(A)$ for some $A\in \mathsf{hIL}$.
Let $x = (a,b)$ and $y = (d,e)$ for some $a,b,d,e \in A$ such that $a\wedge b = d\wedge e = 0$.

In order to show 1), suppose that $x\rightarrow y = 1$, so $a\leq d$, i.e., $x\vee \mathsf{c} \leq y\vee \mathsf{c}$.
Now we will show 2). Suppose that $x\vee \mathsf{c} = y\vee \mathsf{c}$, i.e., $a = d$.
Then $x\rightarrow y = (a\rightarrow d,a\wedge e) =(a\rightarrow a, d\wedge e) = (1,0)$, which is 2). 
Now, assume that $(x\wedge y) \rightarrow 0 = 1$, so $(a\wedge d) \rightarrow 0 =1$. Hence, $a\wedge d = 0$,
which implies that $0\rightarrow (x\wedge y) = 1$ and $x\wedge y \leq \mathsf{c}$. Finally we will prove 4).
A direct computation shows that $(0,0) \rightarrow (0,1) = (1,0)$.
head: environment

label: ce2
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose that $\rho$ is surjective. Let $x, y \in T$ such that $(x\wedge y)\rightarrow 0 = 1$,
so it follows from Lemma \ref{ce1} that $0\rightarrow (x\wedge y) = 1$.
Thus, $x/\theta \wedge y/\theta = 0/\theta$. Since $\rho$ is surjective, there exists $z\in T$
such that $z/\theta = x/\theta$ and $\sim z/\theta = y/\theta$, i.e., 
$z\rightarrow x = 1$, $x\rightarrow z = 1$, $\sim z \rightarrow y = 1$, $y \rightarrow \sim z = 1$. Applying
again Lemma \ref{ce1} we get $z\vee \mathsf{c} = x\vee \mathsf{c}$ and $\sim z \vee \mathsf{c} = y\vee \mathsf{c}$.

Conversely, suppose that $\mathsf{(C)}$ is satisfied and let $x,y \in T$ such that 
$x/\theta \wedge y/\theta = 0/\theta$, so $(x\wedge y)\rightarrow 0 = 1$. It follows from
hypothesis that there exists $z\in T$ such that $z\vee \mathsf{c} = x\vee \mathsf{c}$ and 
$\sim z \vee \mathsf{c} = y\vee \mathsf{c}$. Then it follows from Lemma \ref{ce1} that $z\rightarrow x = 1$, $x\rightarrow z = 1$, 
$\sim z \rightarrow y = 1$ and $y\rightarrow \sim z = 1$. Then $\rho(z) = (x/\theta, y/\theta)$. 
Therefore, $\rho$ is surjective.
head: environment

label: ce3
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{ce3}
Let $T\in \mathsf{KhIL}^{c}$. Conditions $\mathsf{(C)}$ and $\mathsf{(CK)}$ are equivalent.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose that $T$ satisfies $\mathsf{(CK)}$ and let $x, y\in T$ such that $(x\wedge y)\rightarrow 0 = 1$.
It follows from Lemma \ref{ce1} that $x\wedge y \leq \mathsf{c}$. Let $\hat{x} = x\vee \mathsf{c}$ and
$\hat{y} = y\vee \mathsf{c}$. Then $\hat{x}, \hat{y}\geq \mathsf{c}$ and $\hat{x}\wedge \hat{y} \leq \mathsf{c}$,
so it follows from hypothesis that there exists $z\in T$ such that $z\vee \mathsf{c} = \hat{x}$ 
and $\sim z \vee \mathsf{c} = \hat{y}$, i.e., $z\vee \mathsf{c} = x\vee \mathsf{c}$ and $\sim z \vee \mathsf{c} = y\vee \mathsf{c}$.

Conversely, suppose that $\mathsf{(C)}$ is satisfied. Let $x,y\in T$ such that 
$x, y\geq \mathsf{c}$ and $x\wedge y\leq \mathsf{c}$. It follows that $x\wedge y=\mathsf{c}$. It follows from Lemma \ref{ce1} that
$(x\wedge y)\rightarrow 0 = 1$. Thus, it follows from hypothesis that there exists
$z\in T$ such that $z\vee \mathsf{c} = x\vee \mathsf{c}$ and $\sim z \vee \mathsf{c} = y\vee \mathsf{c}$, i.e.,
$z\vee \mathsf{c} = x$ and $\sim z \vee \mathsf{c} = y$.
head: environment

title: Theorem
body_md:
Let $T\in \mathsf{KhIL}$. Then $T$ is isomorphic to $\mathrm{K}(A)$ for some h-lattice $A$
if and only if $T$ has center and satisfies the condition $\mathsf{(CK)}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose that $T \cong \mathrm{K}(A)$ for some $A\in \mathsf{hIL}$. Let $x, y \in \mathrm{K}(A)$ such that
$x, y \geq \mathsf{c}$ and $x\wedge y \leq \mathsf{c}$. Thus, there exist $a,b \in A$ such
that $x = (a,0)$, $y = (b,0)$ and $a\wedge b=0$. The element $z = (a,b) \in \mathrm{K}(A)$ satisfies that  
$z\vee \mathsf{c} = x$ and $\sim z \vee \mathsf{c} = y$. Hence, $\mathrm{K}(A)$ satisfies $\mathsf{(CK)}$. Since this condition
is preserved by isomorphisms then $T$ satisfies $\mathsf{(CK)}$. Furthermore, the fact that $\mathrm{K}(A)$ has center,
which is $(0,0)$, implies that $T$ has center. The converse follows from Lemma \ref{ce2},
Lemma \ref{ce3} and Remark \ref{rem-c}.
head: environment

label: alpha
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We write $\alpha$ in place of $\alpha_{A}$.
First we will show that $\alpha$ is a well defined map. Let $a\in A$. Then $a\wedge (a \rightarrow 0) \leq 0$,
i.e., $a\wedge (a\rightarrow 0) = 0$. 
Thus, $(a, a\rightarrow 0)/\theta \in \mathrm{K}(A)/\theta$.
Let $a\in A$. Then $(a,a\rightarrow 0) /\theta = (a,0)/\theta$. 
It is immediate that $\alpha$ is a homomorphism. 
The injectivity of $\alpha$ is also immediate. 
In order to show that $\alpha$ is suryective, let $y\in \mathsf{C}(\mathrm{K}(A))$, so $y = (a,b)/\theta$
for some $a, b\in A$ such that $a \wedge b = 0$. Moreover, $y = (a, a\rightarrow 0)/\theta$,
so $y = \alpha(a)$. Thus, $\alpha$ is suryective. Therefore, $\alpha$ is an isomorphism.
head: environment

label: center
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
An algebra $\langle H, \wedge, \vee, \rightarrow, 0, 1\rangle$ of type $(2,2,2,0,0)$ is a
\textit{semi-Heyting algebra} if the following conditions hold for
every $a,b,d$ in $H$:
\begin{enumerate}[{\rm (S1)}]
\item $\langle H, \wedge, \vee, 0, 1 \rangle$ is a bounded lattice,
\item $a\wedge (a\rightarrow b) = a \wedge b$, 
\item $a\wedge (b\rightarrow d) = a \wedge [(a\wedge b) \rightarrow (a\wedge d)]$, 
\item $a\rightarrow a = 1$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Definition
head: environment

title: Proposition
body_md: $\mathsf{SN}\subseteq \mathsf{KhIL}$.
head: environment

label: prop-semi
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop-semi}
Let $A\in \mathsf{hIL}$. Then $A\in \mathsf{SH}$ if and only if $\mathrm{K}(A) \in \mathsf{SN}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $A\in \mathsf{hIL}$. It is immediate that if $A\in \mathsf{SH}$ then $\mathrm{K}(A) \in \mathsf{SN}$.
Conversely, suppose that $\mathrm{K}(A) \in \mathsf{SN}$, so $\mathrm{K}(A)/\theta \in \mathsf{SH}$, where $\theta$ is
the equivalence relation considered in Lemma \ref{l1}. Then, since it follows from Lemma \ref{alpha}
that $A$ is isomorphic to $\mathrm{K}(A)/\theta$ then $A\in \mathsf{SH}$, which was our aim.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
Let $A$ be the h-lattice considered in Example \ref{example1}. Note that
$a\wedge (a\rightarrow 1) = 0$ and $a\wedge 1 = 1$, so $a\wedge (a\rightarrow 1) \neq a\wedge 1$. 
Hence, $A\notin \mathsf{SH}$. Thus, it follows from Proposition \ref{prop-semi}
that $\mathrm{K}(A) \notin \mathsf{SN}$. Therefore, $\mathsf{SN}$ is properly contained in $\mathsf{KhIL}$.
head: environment

label: lem-sh
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem-sh}
Let $A\in \mathsf{SH}$ and $a,b,c,d\in A$.
The following conditions are satisfied:
\begin{enumerate}[\normalfont 1)]
\item If $(a,b), (b,c)\in \mathrm{K}(A)$ then $(a,b)\rightarrow_N (c,d) = (1,0)$ if and only if $a\leq c$.
\item $c\leq (a\rightarrow b) \rightarrow ((a\wedge c)\rightarrow (b\wedge c))$.
\item $c\leq ((a\wedge c)\rightarrow (b\wedge c)) \rightarrow (a\rightarrow b)$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $(a,b), (c,d)\in \mathrm{K}(A)$. Note that $(a,b)\rightarrow_N (c,d) = (a\rightarrow (a\wedge c),a\wedge d)$.
Thus, $(a,b)\rightarrow_N (c,d) = (1,0)$ if and only if $a\rightarrow (a\wedge c) = 1$ and $a\wedge d = 0$.
Taking into account that $a\wedge (a\rightarrow (a\wedge c))= a\wedge c$ and $c\wedge d = 0$,
we have that $(a,b)\rightarrow_N(c,d) = (1,0)$ if and only if $a\leq c$. Hence, condition 1) is satisfied.
Conditions 2) and 3) follows from \cite[Lemma 9]{SM2} and the fact that the equation 
$1\rightarrow x = x$ is satisfied in every semi-Heyting algebra.
head: environment

label: lem-sn
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem-sn}
Let $T\in \mathsf{SN}$ and $x,y,f \in T$.
The following conditions are satisfied:
\begin{enumerate}[\normalfont 1)]
\item $f\rightarrow_N ((x\rightarrow y)\rightarrow ((x\wedge f)\rightarrow (y\wedge f)) = 1$.
\item $f\rightarrow_N ((x\wedge f)\rightarrow (y\wedge f))\rightarrow (x\rightarrow y)) = 1$.
\item $f\rightarrow_N (\sim (x\rightarrow y)\rightarrow \sim ((x\wedge f)\rightarrow (y\wedge f)) = 1$.
\item $f\rightarrow_N (\sim((x\wedge f) \rightarrow (y\wedge f))\rightarrow \sim (x\rightarrow y))=1$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Without loss of generality, we can assume that $T = \mathrm{K}(A)$ for some $A\in \mathsf{SH}$.
Conditions 1) and 2) follow from Lemma \ref{lem-sh}.
The proofs of 3) and 4) follow from a direct computation based on the definition
of semi-Heyting algebras.
head: environment

title: Proposition
body_md:
Let $T\in \mathsf{SN}$. Then the set of h-implicative filters of $T$ coincides
with the set of N-implicative filters of $T$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $T\in \mathsf{SN}$. It follows from Proposition \ref{N-ds}
that every h-implicative filter of $T$
is an N-implicative filter of $T$.
The fact that every N-implicative
filter of $T$ is an h-implicative filter of $T$ follows 
from a direct computation based on Remark \ref{rem-Nsd} and 
Lemma \ref{lem-sn}.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
A \textit{subresiduated lattice} is a pair $(A, D)$, where $A$ 
is a bounded distributive lattice and $D$ is a bounded sublattice of $A$ such 
that for each $a, b \in A$ there exists the maximum of the set $\{d\in D:a\wedge d\leq b\}$. 
This element is denoted by $a\rightarrow b$.
head: environment

title: Definition
head: environment

title: Proposition
body_md: $\mathsf{SNA}\subseteq \mathsf{KhIL}$.
head: environment

label: prop-sna
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop-sna}
Let $A\in \mathsf{hIL}$. Then $A\in \mathsf{SRL}$ if and only if $\mathrm{K}(A) \in \mathsf{SNA}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: It is similar to the proof of Proposition \ref{prop-semi}.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
Let $A$ be the h-lattice considered in Example \ref{example1}. Note that
$(a\vee 0)\rightarrow a =1$ and $(a\rightarrow a) \wedge (0\rightarrow a) = a$,
so $(a\vee 0)\rightarrow a \neq (a\rightarrow a) \wedge (0\rightarrow a)$.
Hence, $A\notin \mathsf{SRL}$. Thus, it follows from Proposition \ref{prop-sna}
that $\mathrm{K}(A) \notin \mathsf{SNA}$, so $\mathsf{SNA}$ is properly contained in $\mathsf{KhIL}$.
head: environment

label: oif=gif
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{oif=gif}
Let $T \in \mathsf{SNA}$ and $x, y,z\in T$. Then the following conditions are satisfied:
\begin{enumerate}[\normalfont 1)]
\item $(x\rightarrow (x\wedge z)) \rightarrow (((x\wedge z) \rightarrow (y\wedge z)) \rightarrow (x\rightarrow y)) = 1$.
\item $(x\rightarrow y) \rightarrow ((x\wedge z) \rightarrow (y\wedge z)) = 1$.
\item $((x\wedge\sim y)\rightarrow \sim ((x\wedge z)\rightarrow y)) \rightarrow(\sim (x\rightarrow y) \rightarrow \sim ((x\wedge z)\rightarrow (y\wedge z)))= 1$.
\item $\sim ((x\wedge z)\rightarrow (y\wedge z))\rightarrow \sim (x\rightarrow y) = 1$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $T \in \mathsf{SNA}$. Without loss of generality we can assume that $T$ 
takes the form $\mathrm{K}(A)$ for some $A\in \mathsf{SRL}$.
In order to show 1), 
it is enough to show that for every $a,b,c \in A$, $a\rightarrow (a\wedge c) \leq ((a\wedge c) \rightarrow (b\wedge c)) \rightarrow (a\rightarrow b)$
\footnote{In \cite[Remark 3.1]{LMSM} it was shown that if $A\in \mathsf{SRL}$ and $(a,b), (c,d)\in \mathrm{K}(A)$,
then $(a,b)\rightarrow (c,d) = (1,0)$ if and only if $a\leq c$.}.
The last equality holds if and only if $(a\rightarrow (a\wedge c)) \wedge ((a\wedge c) \rightarrow (b\wedge c)) \leq a\rightarrow b$. This follows from the fact that $a\rightarrow (b\wedge c)\leq a\rightarrow b$. 

That conditions 2), 3) and 4) are satisfied
follows from a direct computation.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
Every open implicative filter of a subresiduated Nelson algebra is an upset.
Indeed, let $T \in \mathsf{SNA}$ and let $F$ be an open implicative filter of $T$.
Let $x,y \in T$ be such that $x \leq y$ and $x \in F$. Then, it is easy to show that $x \rightarrow y = 1$. Since $x,x\rightarrow y \in F$, it follows that $y \in F$.
head: environment

title: Proposition
body_md:
Let $T\in \mathsf{SNA}$. Then the set of h-implicative filters of $T$ coincides
with the set of open implicative filters of $T$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $T\in \mathsf{SNA}$. It follows from Proposition \ref{open-if}
that every h-implicative filter of $T$
is an open implicative filter of $T$. The fact that every open implicative
filter of $T$ satisfies F1) and F4) follows 
from a direct computation based on Lemma \ref{oif=gif}. 

Let $F$ be an open implicative filter of $T$. To prove that it satisfies F2) suppose that $z\in F$. Then, $x\rightarrow (x\wedge z)=(x\rightarrow x)\wedge (x\rightarrow z)=x\rightarrow z$. Since $x\leq 1$, we obtain $1\rightarrow z\leq x\rightarrow z$ and from the fact that $1\rightarrow z\in F$, we obtain $x\rightarrow z\in F$. From Lemma \ref{oif=gif}, $(x\rightarrow (x\wedge z)) \rightarrow (((x\wedge z) \rightarrow (y\wedge z)) \rightarrow (x\rightarrow y)) \in F$ and thus $((x\wedge z) \rightarrow (y\wedge z)) \rightarrow (x\rightarrow y) \in F$.
To prove that $F$ satisfies F3), suppose that $z\in F$.
